variants.reconstruction:
%n attā | tattakkip-ma || kīma lēʾim | tušabraqšu
#note: See @bib{RN117@244}: “The line divides into two equal halves, with a pause at the caesura: @i{átta} | @i{tattakkípma} || @i{kīma lé’im} | @i{tušabráqšu}. The bull belongs with the second verb. Renger read @i{tušaprakšu} and translated ‘als war er ein Ringer, wirst [Du] ihm (den Hals) zur Seite drehen’; this is perhaps reading too much into @i{šupruku}, ‘to put in the way’. Hecker follows Renger but I side with Bottéro, Tournay and Shaffer, who render the clause ‘tu l’abattras comme un taureau’. The bull develops the imagery of the first part of the line in a way that a wrestler would not. The causative stem of @i{barāqu} is used figuratively for violent destruction of an enemy: see the passages quoted in @i{CAD} B, p. 104, 2 c, and note @i{Malku} I 107: @i{šub-ru-qu} = @i{da-a-ku}, ‘to kill’ (@bib{temp_id_2401129561684543@426}).”

#note: See @bib{RN117@244}: “The significance of forcing the bull’s head down (flat on the ground?) is probably that this is how a bull-wrestler breaks a bull’s neck. Contra Hecker, @i{TUAT} III/4, p. 661, fn. 6a, @i{rēšīšu} is not plural but dual, as often.”

%n bāni | qaqqadīka | lugalbanda
#note: See @bib{RN117@245}: “As W. G. Lambert tells me (private communication), the phrase @i{bāni qaqqadim} in the meaning ‘father, sire’ is a calque from Sumerian @sux{sag.du₃} (var. @sux{du/dug₄}), for which see G. R. Castellino, @i{Two Šulgi Hymns (BC)}, p. 181; Å. W. Sjöberg, @i{TCS} III, p. 54. Note especially in an inscription of Samsuiluna: @sux{{d}nanna dingir sag.du.mu.še₃} : @akk{a-na {d}EN:[ZU] DINGIR ba-ni-ia}, ‘for Sîn, the god who begot me’ (D. Frayne, @i{RIME} 4, p. 381, 41–2 // 39).”

variants.reconstruction:
%n etqet | eli šalaštin | šunātīya
#note: See @bib{RN117@245–246}: “For a @i{plene} spelling comparable to @akk{e-et-qe₃-et}, and from the same verb, see the imperative  @akk{e-et-qa₂-ni-i-ma}, ‘pass me by!’, in the OB narrative poem about Narām-Sîn and Apišal (v 7; @bib{RN262@182}). The form @i{šalaštin} compares, as Renger noted, with @i{erbettin} in @akk{ki-ib-ra-a-at er-be₂-ti-in}, ‘four world-regions’, in a fragmentary OB text about Sargon of Akkade (@i{BRM} IV 4, 4–5, ed. @bib{RN262@34}). The parallel is more instructive than Renger saw, however, for the gender of the number is the same as the noun. The absence of polarity thus marks the phrase @i{šalaštin šunātīya} as comprising two nouns, though in apposition rather than in a possessive construction such as @i{kibrāt/sūq/šār erbettim}. Usual language would yield @i{šalāš šunātīya}. @i{šalaštum} is a group of three (‘triad’) comparable with @i{erbettum}, ‘group of four’, @i{ḫamiltu}, ‘group of five’, and @i{sebettum}, ‘heptad’. For nunation in OB see now @i{GAG}³ §§44c (possessive pronouns), 63c (miscellaneous).”

lines.translation: #tr.en: it surpasses my (other) three dreams!

lines.translation: #tr.en: I watched an Anzû-bird in the sky,

variants.reconstruction:
%n itbē-ma | kīma erpeti || išaʾʾu | elni
#note: See @bib{RN117@245–246}: “At the beginning of the line the reading @i{itbēma} (against Renger: @akk{š[a] x x}), which Bottéro (‘il s’élança’, also Tournay and Shaffer) and Hecker (‘er erhob sich’) also saw, means that @i{i-ša-ú} is not the present subjunctive of the ‘hollow’ root √@i{šūʾ}, but the plain present of a variant II+III-Aleph root (@i{u/u}). As Renger noted, @i{šâ’u} also describes the characteristic behaviour of the mythical lion-headed eagle, the @i{Anzû}-bird, in an inscription of Aššurnaṣirpal II (now Grayson, @i{RIMA} 2, p. 260, 74). The verb seems to cover soaring, wheeling and swooping, that is, the flight pattern typical of large birds of prey. Division of the poetic line into units indicates that the simile occurs before the caesura and so belongs in the first clause not the second: @i{itbēma} | @i{kīma érpetim} || @i{išáʾʾu} | @i{elīni}.

variants.reconstruction:
%n šalummassa | tapallaham | attā
#note: See @bib{RN117@246 ad 4′–5′}: “The structure of the couplet is enhanced by the opposition of @i{atta} and @i{anāku}. The first word of l. 5' remains a problem. Renger proposed derivation from @i{etēmum}, and translated ‘werde ich @i{anstoßen}’, but the meaning of this verb is very obscure. A more secure candidate is @i{ṭênum} (@akk{e-ṭe₄-en}, ‘I shall mill’), but the sense leaves a lot to be desired. The unusual spelling of @i{ušetbēka} recalls the use of CV signs for VC in an older tradition of orthography, as for example at Ebla. On this see below, the introduction to OB Harmal₂.”
